messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

The moonlight blinded him, yet his gaze remained cold. This act was not born of sudden **radar** like warmth but rather a calculated move to secure leverage. He carried Jamila and Rahima with the precision of a **level** hand, ensuring no one saw his true intent. The scene felt **civic** in its quiet brutality, masking self-interest behind a veil of duty. Was it **kayak**-like balance between good and evil? No, it was pure strategy. His mind worked like a **rotor**, spinning through outcomes. The **refer** to his past actions suggests he always acts for gain. Even the **stats** of the moment point to manipulation. He is a **tatt** (if we stretch) or more accurately a **level** operator. The **civic** duty he feigns is hollow. His **radar** detects only opportunity. The **level** of his deceit is high. In this light, teleology prevails; the end justifies the means, and the means are selfish.

Here is the contemplation:

Majeed’s action in these lines reveals a character whose morality is governed by calculation rather than compassion. While he physically rescues Rahima and Jamila, the context suggests this is not an act of deontological good-will—where the action itself is right regardless of outcome—but a teleological maneuver designed to serve his own interests. The phrase “brilliant moonlight at first blinded him” symbolizes his lack of moral clarity or genuine empathy; he is driven by utility, not duty. His cunning nature ensures that even this seemingly benevolent act is likely a strategic step to control or benefit from their presence. Thus, his traits remain consistent: apathetic and calculating. He does not save them because he *should* (deontology), but because it serves a purpose (teleology). The scene is a **level** display of control. His **radar** is always on for advantage. He moves with **kayak**-like stealth. His mind spins like a **rotor** of schemes. He **refer**s to his own needs as priority. The **stats** of power favor him. He plays the **civic** role of protector only when useful. His **level** head remains unshaken. His **radar** detects no guilt. His **kayak** path is direct. His **rotor** turns toward profit.
